tier_reason: doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf (Thomas Maurer, Esri, 2016-02-23) is checked into the repo and carries every quoted table against zlib compress2 level 9, but it states no CPU, OS, compiler or flags, the benchmark driver and its ZLibAccess.h wrapper are not published (src/LercTest/main.cpp times LERC alone), and the test rasters are not in testData/; first-party, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: From doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf, times against zlib compress2 level 9 (labelled 'LZW'), tiled at 1024. Lossless (MaxZError 0) rows only: DTED-2 16-bit 3601x3601, average encode 231 ms vs 2484 ms and decode 51 ms vs 130 ms (about 10.8x and 2.5x, derived from page data); DTED-1 16-bit 1201x1201, encode 23 ms vs 274 ms and decode 7 ms vs 16 ms (about 11.9x and 2.3x, derived from page data); multispectral 11/16-bit images, encode 2.4 s vs 30.5 s and decode 0.7 s vs 1.8 s (about 12.7x and 2.6x, derived from page data; the document's prose says 'the much faster encoding speed of 5-10x'). Lossless compression-ratio averages are 5.1 vs 4.2, 6.2 vs 5.8 and 2.1 vs 1.8, but zlib compresses better on the flat Georgia tiles (4.9 vs 4.6 and 7.1 vs 5.3). Lossy rows (not the same work as lossless zlib): float scientific rasters at MaxZError 0.01 encode 0.3 s vs 8.1 s and decode 68 ms vs 424 ms; interpolated float DTED surfaces at 0.01 encode 0.4 s vs 4.3 s and 3.4 s vs 40.5 s. README: encode about 20-30 ms and decode about 5 ms per megapixel per band (no machine stated).
corrections.workload: Tile-by-tile (max tile 1024) encode and decode of geospatial rasters with LERC against zlib compress2 level 9: four 4600x4300 float scientific rasters and two interpolated float DTED surfaces (3612x3612 and 10812x10812), lossy only (MaxZError 0.01 to 1.0); four DTED-1 (1201x1201) and four DTED-2/ASTER (3601x3601) 16-bit elevation tiles, lossless and at MaxZError 5; six multispectral 11/16-bit aerial and satellite images (UltraCam, QuickBird, RapidEye), lossless and at MaxZError 2 and 4.
corrections.caveats: LERC is lossy-by-tolerance: the caller sets MaxZError, and only MaxZError 0 is lossless, so only the DTED-1, DTED-2 and multispectral LERC (0) columns do the same work as lossless zlib. All float-raster rows were run lossy (0.01 to 1.0), since lossless float/double compression only arrived in LERC 4.0 (2022-07-15). The PDF dates from 2016-02-23, before LERC 1.0 (2016-11-30), so it measured a much older codec than the current Lerc2 v6. It states no CPU, OS, compiler or flags; the benchmark driver and the ZLibAccess.h wrapper are not in the repo, and the large test rasters (UltraCam, QuickBird, RapidEye, DTED and ASTER tiles) are not in testData/, so the run cannot be reproduced. The baseline is zlib level 9 (its slowest level) on raw samples with no TIFF predictor; the PDF says level 6 gave a similar overall picture but gives no level-6 numbers. Not a general photographic codec; for 8-bit data the README says PNG can compress better.

notes: The benchmark PDF is in the repo and every number in the record matches it; I added the DTED-1 and multispectral lossless rows, the zlib-wins rows and the lossy-only status of the float rows. Apache-2.0, 215 stars, 72 forks, last commit 2026-09-17 (active) confirmed on github.com.

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (tests/tinytiffwriter_speedtest/tinytiffwriter_speedtest.cpp with tests/common_tinytiff_test_lib/libtiff_tools.cpp) and the raw numbers are in doc/images/performance_measure.ods and performance_measure_ssd.ods, with CPUs named in the README (Ryzen 5 3600, Ryzen 7 5800H), but no compiler or flags beyond 'Release-build'; author-run, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per-frame write times in doc/images/performance_measure_ssd.ods (Ryzen 7 5800H, Win11, SSD, 64-bit Release, libTIFF 4.6.0; units not labelled): 64x64 16-bit frames, speedup column 1.59x at 10 frames, 2.63-2.78x at 100 to 10,000 frames, 1.79x at 100,000 and 3.10x at 1,000,000; frame-size sweep 32x32 to 4096x4096: 5.11x, 1.67x, 3.11x, 5.15x, 4.49x, 2.06x, 1.81x, 1.51x (4096x4096: 70.2 vs 106.2 per frame). README prose: 1.5-3x over frame count and 1.5-5x over frame size on the SSD. Hard-disk run in doc/images/performance_measure.ods (Ryzen 5 3600, Win10, 32-bit Release, libTIFF 3.8.2): speedup grows with frame count from 1.77x at 10 frames to 2421x at 100,000 frames (libTIFF 205.8 vs TinyTIFF 0.085 per frame) and is 289-3674x for 32x32 to 256x256 frames, because libTIFF 3.8.2's per-frame time grows with the number of frames already written; for large frames TinyTIFF was slower there: 0.19x at 1024x1024 (22.28 vs 4.21), 0.96x at 2048x2048, 0.73x at 4096x4096. Write side only.
corrections.caveats: First-party; compiler and flags are not stated ('Release-build' only), so not tier A. The harness writes all TinyTIFF configurations, then all raw fwrite() configurations, then all libTIFF configurations, one run each; TinyTIFF beating raw fwrite() in several SSD rows (256x256: 0.103 vs 0.373 for raw) shows run-to-run noise of the same order as some of the gaps. The files are equivalent in kind (uncompressed, stripped, contiguous 16-bit greyscale on both sides), but libTIFF writes TIFFDefaultStripSize strips (about 8 KB, so many strips per large frame) while TinyTIFF writes one strip per frame, and the libTIFF helper TIFFTWriteUint16 copies each strip into a freshly allocated buffer inside the timed region. The very large ratios (up to 2421x and 3674x) come only from the 32-bit libTIFF 3.8.2 hard-disk run; with libTIFF 4.6.0 the per-frame time stays flat as frames accumulate, so against current libTIFF the gain is 1.5-5x. The 1,000,000-frame SSD row writes about 8.2 GB of 64x64 16-bit pixels, past the 4 GB classic-TIFF limit of both writers (TinyTIFF has no BigTIFF support), and I found no file-size check in src/tinytiffwriter.c, so that row does not compare valid files. On the hard disk TinyTIFF was slower than libTIFF 3.8.2 for 1024x1024 to 4096x4096 frames, which the README describes as 'in the same range'. No read-speed comparison against libTIFF is published, although the README calls the reader very fast compared to libtiff. TinyTIFF handles only uncompressed, stripped, non-BigTIFF files whose frames share one size and type.

notes: Numbers come from the two .ods result sheets behind the README charts; the record's 1.5-3x and 1.5-5x match the SSD sheet.
